Seamanship · Issue 14

Notes from a Night Watch at Anchor

What you learn about a harbor between midnight and four, when the wind backs and the moon goes down.

IH
Ines Halloran10 November 2026 · 6 min read

The night watch at anchor is not really a watch. Nobody is steering. Nothing is supposed to happen. You sit in the cockpit with a mug of something warm, check the anchor alarm, look at the transits you took at dusk, and listen to the harbor breathe.

And it does breathe. Around one, the land breeze starts to slide down off the hills, and every boat in the bay swings slowly to face it, like a field of compasses. Around two, the last bar in town turns its lights off. Around three, if the tide is right, you hear the ebb begin to chuckle along the hull.

The thing you learn, sitting there, is that a harbor is never really still. It is just quiet enough, for a few hours, to let you notice everything that moves. ■
